Go solo with self-directed investing,

Whatever trails you take,

This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington,
I'm Dave Mattingly.
Markets in Asia are down today
following yesterday's sell-off on Wall Street.
The Dow lost more than 3%.
The S&P 500 finished more than 4% lower.
The NASDAQ lost more than 5.5%.
Analysts say investors are concerned
about Congress putting more restrictions
on artificial intelligence and data center build-outs
when Democrats retake control
of the House and Senate come January.
A day after Democrats won sweeping victories in the midterms,
a Republican congressman is threatening
to re-introduce articles of impeachment
against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Thomas Massey of Kentucky says he'll do so
unless Hegseth resigns.
In a video statement, Hegseth cited the previous impeachments
of President Trump in the House,
saying they failed to stop Trump,
and Hegseth added they won't stop him.
Their policies don't work,
so their obsession with political theater
disguised as power drives them
to try to destroy their opponents.
It's all about the politics of personal destruction.
Massey has been critical of Hegseth
in part because of the war with Iran.
The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division
is stepping down after 18 months on the job.
As NPR's Ryan Lucas reports,
Harvey Dillon is the first senior DOJ official to leave
following the Democrats' sweeping election wins.
Attorney General Todd Blanche announced in a post on X
that he had accepted Dillon's resignation.
He said she had defended civil liberties
and enforced the law without fear or favor.
During her tenure,
Dillon radically reshaped the Civil Rights Division
and its mission.
She pushed out hundreds of career attorneys
and replaced them with inexperienced ideological allies.
Current and former division attorneys also say
she shifted the unit's enforcement mission
from protecting civil rights
to instead focusing on advancing President Trump's
MAGA agenda.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Exit polls examining the religious vote
in Tuesday's midterm elections
show higher support for Democratic candidates
among those with no religious affiliation.
NPR's Jason Derose says the polls also show
more Catholics move toward Democrats.
Nearly eight in 10 religiously unaffiliated voters
went for Democrats during the midterms
according to the voter poll conducted by SSRS.
Catholic voters were evenly divided
between Republicans and Democrats this year
after breaking for GOP candidates in 2024.
Support for Democrats among Jewish voters
appears to be softening.
The voter poll found that about seven in 10
went for Democrats in the midterms,
while that number was nearly eight in 10 two years ago.
Just prior to the election,
Pew Research found that the economy
was the overriding issue for voters
regardless of religious affiliation.
Jason Derose, NPR News.
This is NPR News from Washington.
Pope Leo is visiting Latin America
over the next week and a half.
The Pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru
less than a month after he underwent surgery
for lung cancer.
The Vatican says the Pope's doctors
cleared him to make the trip.
Latin America is home to about 40% of the world's Catholics.
There's been a major political development
in the Kurdistan region of Iraq.
NPR's Jana Raff says one of two main political parties
has announced its withdrawing from the regional government
and is threatening to form a breakaway administration.
The Kurdistan region is part of Iraq,
but it's semi-autonomous, and it has its own parliament.
The two main political parties
control different parts of the region,
and they've long been rivals.
The head of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan,
Bafel Talabani, announced his party was withdrawing
from the regional government
after a two-year-long dispute over government posts.
He threatened to create a separate administration
in areas his party controls.
Tensions are already high due to continued attacks by Iran,
which is targeting armed Iranian Kurdish opposition groups
in Iraq's Kurdistan region and following the withdrawal
of U.S. forces from Iraq in September.
Jana Raff, NPR News, Amman.
Authorities in Canada say they're still searching
for the grizzly bear that killed a mother and daughter
in British Columbia.
Their remains were found near a trail
not far from where a grizzly bear
attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year.
That attack left 11 people injured at least two critically.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.
